A Comprehensive Profit Evaluation of Modern Cinema

Author

Liam Boyd, Matt Schneider

Published

December 7, 2024

Question to Answer:

When assuming an unlimited access to investment funds and planning to produce a movie, what factors represent profitability? What should be considered when picking what style of movie you should create?

Summary

  • Through clustering analysis, the ideal movie to invest in is a mid-budget film to maximize profits. This minimizes the risk involved with low-budget films, and generally produces higher overall profits relative to the budget spent on production when compared to high-budget films.

  • Through careful analysis, we have found that there is little correlation between a movie’s profit ratio, genre, post-production ratings and seasonal release date. These imply that a producer may choose to tailor their film to personal preference and potentially put more of a focus on the ideal cast involved.

  • There are many external factors not considered in our analysis to maximize profits. This generally stems from inaccessible data, and other qualitative factors that audiences consider such as brand loyalty and movie marketing.

Analysis

Clustering Analysis

Through clustering analysis we first use the elbow method to determine the ideal amount of clusters. For each k value we calculate the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), and plot it to determine the ideal k where there is a marginal change in WCSS. The ideal number of clusters according to our graph is ~3, implying that there are three distinct groups in our data set with clear differences in budget, run time, and profitability.

Cluster 1:

  • Lowest budget films have the greatest variation in profitability though the average budget of $4.6M returns an average profit of (44.7x) return. This means that this cluster can be highly profitable despite the smaller scale productions.

  • This cluster has the smallest amount of movies produced, showing that these films are rare but can be extremely financially successful.

  • The variation seen on the graph demonstrates the high risk involved due to the large spread of films having many different results when similar budgets and run times are considered.

Cluster 2:

  • This group represents high-budget films with an average budget of $133M and the longest average run times (135 minutes).

  • This is the lowest profit ratio (2.4x) of the three clusters, indicating that these films are likely higher risk, high investment projects that yield lower returns.

  • Considering that there are nearly 600 movies in this data set, this indicates that many high-budget films struggle to achieve significant profits.

Cluster 3:

  • This group represents medium-budget films with an average budget of $33M with the shortest average run time (107 minutes)

  • This group generates the highest profit per dollar invested (3.5x) of the three clusters.

  • Considering that this is the largest cluster, this shows that it is the most common category and the most ideal for investment.

Movie Genre Significance

As seen by our analysis above, budget does have an effect on the profitability of a movie. Is there any other factors that we could include in our best model of predicting profit ratio with the data available? We ran a PCA analysis on genre and concluded the following.

Limited Predictive Power of Genres: The first principle component (PC1), which represents the most significant variation in genres, showed a very weak correlation with ProfitRatio (r = 0.0178). This suggests that genres contribute minimally to explaining or predicting movie profitability.

Seasonality Regression

Through a simple linear regression model, it can be noticed that there is no significance on the release date of the movie throughout the year.

  • Each coefficient has a high p-value, showing that none of the seasons are significant factors of a movie’s profitability.

  • The low R-Squared value represents that the release date represents nearly 0% of variance in profit ratio.
